pages.title: Language research and the Cognitive Revolution
Language as a formal symbolic system
pages.c: **The Cognitive Revolution brought internal mental representations back into explanations of language.** A formal account describes language through abstract symbols and rules. This contrasts with the behaviorist goal of explaining learning through relations among observable stimuli, responses, and consequences. Skinner’s Verbal Behavior attempted to explain language through operant conditioning, while Chomsky’s 1959 critique challenged whether that approach could explain linguistic knowledge.
support: Experimental psychology in the 1950s and 1960s often resisted explanations that appealed to an internal state. The debate therefore concerned what an explanation was allowed to contain, as well as which particular learning process produced speech.
A grammar is an internal system that can characterize sentences a person has never encountered. Taking that system seriously made language a central case for a psychology of mental structure.
pages.d: The central change was to treat an unobservable representation as something that could be investigated through its consequences. A theory could ask what knowledge a speaker must have to produce and understand language, rather than describing only the environmental conditions associated with a response.

pages.title: Computers and the question of intelligence
pages.c: **General-purpose computation made machine intelligence a serious theoretical question.** Early computers could perform many kinds of calculation and logical operation, rather than a single fixed task. Alan Turing’s wartime work on decryption formed part of the historical setting for asking whether manipulating information in a machine could resemble human thought.
support: A machine’s ability to carry out different formal operations encouraged researchers to describe cognition as information processing. The important comparison concerns what processes a system performs and how it produces intelligent behavior.

This question connects language research with artificial intelligence. If language can be represented using symbols and procedures, a computer becomes a way to explore what those representations and procedures can accomplish.
pages.d: The historical argument starts from flexibility. A general-purpose machine can run different procedures on different information, so researchers can ask whether the difference between it and a human is a difference in the procedures, the representations, or something else.

pages.title: The Turing test and the imitation game
pages.c: **The Turing test evaluates a machine through conversational behavior.** In the original imitation-game setup, A and B are a man and a woman, and C is an examiner trying to determine their genders. One participant tries to mislead the examiner while the other helps. The machine version asks whether a computer can replace a participant without the examiner recognizing the substitution.
support: The examiner has to infer the identity of the conversational partner from the responses. Successful performance therefore depends on producing answers that fit the interaction, rather than simply displaying an isolated computational skill.
The test turns the broad question of intelligence into a comparison of observable conversational performance. Natural language is the medium through which the examiner makes that judgment.
pages.d: The machine is evaluated from the examiner’s position. The examiner does not inspect its circuitry or program and instead decides what kind of partner could have produced the conversation. The relevant outcome is whether the substitution is detected.
pages.visual: A and B identify the two respondents, while C identifies the examiner. The roles matter because one respondent may deliberately mislead C. The cartoon about persuading the examiner that the examiner is a computer plays on this role of deception.

pages.title: Language and learning in Turing’s proposal
pages.c: **Turing’s proposal emphasizes ordinary language use and learning rather than a single expert performance.** Producing a large calculation or composing poetry is different from sustaining the broad conversational behavior that the imitation game requires. A respondent also has to handle the possibility that an examiner is trying to expose its identity.
support: Turing’s developmental suggestion was to begin with something possessing a child’s cognitive capabilities and allow it to learn toward adult performance. On this proposal, intelligence develops through experience rather than being supplied as a finished list of adult answers.
pages.d: Natural language joins the different demands of the test. A conversational partner must interpret questions, choose relevant information, and produce an appropriate response. Learning provides a proposed route to acquiring that flexibility, rather than building a separate fixed response for every possible exchange.

pages.title: General Problem Solver and symbolic search
pages.c: **Newell and Simon’s General Problem Solver treats a problem as symbols and procedures for changing them.** Once a task is represented formally, the system can search for operations that transform the current state into a goal state. Games, puzzles, geometry proofs, and algebraic word problems provide settings where the states and permitted operations can be specified explicitly.
support: The Tower of Hanoi is useful because a configuration of disks can be described as a state and a legal move produces another state. A solution is a sequence of permitted changes that reaches the required configuration.
This illustrates the GOFAI approach, in which intelligent behavior is modeled as operations on explicit symbolic representations.
pages.d: The search depends on the representation. The program must have a way to distinguish states, identify a goal, and choose legal transformations. Once these are specified, solving the problem becomes finding a successful path through the possible transformations.
pages.visual: The Tower of Hanoi diagram connects disk configurations into a state space. A connection represents a permitted move between configurations. The branching pattern makes alternative routes through the problem visible.

pages.title: Why early AI favored formal problems
pages.c: **Early AI’s focus on formal problems reflected both technical constraints and theoretical commitments.** Punchcards and machine-language input made it easier to supply explicit symbols than rich perceptual information. A task such as finding a face in a detailed image was consequently much harder to present to a computer than a formally described puzzle.
support: Theoretical commitments also mattered. Rational goal-directed reasoning was treated as a particularly revealing form of intelligence. A system that represents a goal and chooses procedures for reaching it makes that form of reasoning explicit.

Training an organism to produce useful behavior and giving a program an explicit representation of a goal are different explanatory approaches. The contrast concerns how the successful behavior is produced.
pages.d: A formal puzzle already comes organized into states, goals, and rules. Everyday perception requires a system to work out useful structure from the incoming information itself. Favoring the first kind of task therefore also shaped the kinds of intelligence early programs modeled.

pages.title: Chomsky’s critique of a conditioning account
pages.c: **Chomsky argued that language knowledge includes an internal grammar that supports novel sentences.** Speakers distinguish sentences from nonsentences, interpret new combinations, and recognize ambiguity. His critique proposed that a set of abstract structural principles characterizes these abilities more successfully than simple similarity to previously reinforced utterances.
support: The argument concerns productivity. A person can understand and judge an expression without having heard that exact expression before. An explanation must account for the structure that makes this possible.

Chomsky also drew attention to children’s rapid acquisition of complex grammars. He treated this as evidence for specialized capacities to organize linguistic input and formulate hypotheses about its structure.
pages.d: The contrast is between matching a new utterance to a familiar example and assigning it a structural analysis. In the grammar account, a new sentence is possible because it can be generated and interpreted through the system the speaker has internalized.

pages.title: Grammaticality judgments and productivity
pages.c: **A generative grammar characterizes an open-ended set of sentences using a finite system of abstract rules.** The speaker’s knowledge extends beyond expressions already encountered. Grammaticality judgments are important evidence in this tradition because a person can judge a completely new sentence as well formed or ill formed.
support: An individual sentence is one product of the system. The theoretical target is the system that makes many possible sentences available and assigns their structure.
Understanding ambiguity also requires structure. The same sequence can receive more than one analysis, so recognizing the words alone does not determine the complete interpretation.
pages.d: The appeal to judgments changes the main research question. Instead of asking only which utterances a person has produced, a researcher asks which structures the person recognizes as possible in the language and which distinctions those judgments reveal.

pages.title: The challenge to stimulus generalization
pages.c: **Chomsky challenged the idea that grammatical novelty can be explained by simple stimulus generalization.** In conditioning, a response may extend from a trained stimulus to another that resembles it. His argument was that the abstract relation among grammatical sentences cannot be reduced to an obvious similarity in sound, meaning, or a familiar sentence frame.
support: A grammatical system can license new combinations whose components and meanings differ greatly from familiar utterances. The issue is how a learner recognizes the structural relation that makes the combination possible.
In this account, a sentence is recognized because it belongs to the system the person has internalized. Resemblance to one remembered utterance is not the proposed basis for that judgment.
pages.d: The disagreement concerns the kind of generalization being explained. Extending a trained response to a similar physical stimulus and recognizing an abstract grammatical relation are not automatically the same process. A language theory has to explain the latter relation.

pages.title: Generalization gradients in conditioning
pages.c: **A conditioned response can generalize according to similarity between stimuli.** When a pigeon is trained to peck in response to a green light, it may also peck at nearby colors. Responding is strongest around the trained stimulus and decreases as the test color becomes less similar. This is a generalization gradient.
support: Color and numerical magnitude provide relatively concrete dimensions along which stimuli can vary. A training procedure can establish which response is reinforced and then measure how that response changes across test stimuli.
The challenge for a conditioning account of language is to identify what corresponds to this similarity dimension for an abstract grammatical relationship.
pages.d: The gradient connects a controlled change in the stimulus with a change in behavior. It is not simply a claim that learning transfers. It specifies that transfer varies with the relation between the test stimulus and the reinforced stimulus.
pages.visual: The color graph places the greatest response around green and lower response toward other colors. The pigeon photograph concerns a magnitude discrimination task, so it illustrates another dimension of stimulus comparison rather than an additional point on the color graph.

pages.title: Stimulus control as an explanation of verbal behavior
pages.c: **Stimulus control links a response to an aspect of the environment.** In a verbal-behavior account, an environmental event can be treated as the stimulus associated with a spoken response. Music and proper names are examples used in the debate about how far this idea can explain language.
support: The explanatory question is which property of the situation controls the utterance. A piece of music can have many properties, and a speaker can respond to the situation in different ways. A useful account must identify the relevant relation between stimulus and response.
pages.d: Calling an utterance a response to a stimulus begins an explanation only if the relevant stimulus can be identified independently of the utterance. Otherwise the response itself ends up determining what is counted as its cause.

pages.title: Why predicting an utterance differs from explaining grammar
pages.c: **Chomsky objected that a stimulus cannot explain a verbal response if it is identified only after the response occurs.** Social relationships, prior experience, goals, and other cognitive activity all influence what a person chooses to say. Inferring the controlling stimulus from whatever the person said makes the proposed prediction circular.
support: The alternative research target is linguistic structure. A researcher can examine which arrangements speakers produce and accept, then propose a grammar that characterizes those arrangements.
This separates a theory of the structure of possible utterances from a complete theory of why a particular person chooses a particular utterance at a particular moment.
pages.d: The distinction concerns the explanandum, or what the theory is trying to explain. A grammar describes structural possibilities. A full account of speaking in a social situation has to explain the selection of one possibility from many, under influences that extend beyond linguistic structure.

pages.title: Colorless green ideas and grammatical structure
pages.c: **Grammatical structure and meaningfulness can come apart.** “Colorless green ideas sleep furiously” has a recognizable English sentence structure even though its meaning is difficult to interpret literally. Reversing the words into “Furiously sleep ideas green colorless” removes that structure. Chomsky used the contrast to argue that prior exposure to the complete sentence cannot explain the judgment.
support: The ordered sentence places the adjectives before the noun and follows the noun phrase with a verb and an adverb. The reversed version uses the same words but changes their structural relations.

“Car! Getting towed! Yours!” makes the complementary point. A warning can be understandable from its situation even though it is not a complete conventional sentence. Communicative success and grammatical form are separate questions.
pages.d: Keeping the words constant while rearranging them makes word order and structure central to the comparison. The difference is not that one sentence uses familiar words and the other uses unfamiliar words. It is how those words are organized.

pages.title: Marr’s three levels of analysis
pages.c: **Marr distinguished computational, algorithmic, and implementational descriptions of a cognitive system.** The computational level characterizes the problem the system solves. The algorithmic level describes the representations and procedures used to solve it. The implementational level concerns how those procedures are physically realized.
support: These levels distinguish different questions about the same ability. An account of what counts as a successful result is different from an account of the steps used to obtain it or the physical machinery carrying out those steps.
Chomsky’s abstract characterization of linguistic knowledge is interpreted here as a computational description. It characterizes the structural system that language processing must realize.
pages.d: A description can be informative at one level without answering every question at the others. The purpose of separating levels is to make clear whether a claim concerns the task, the procedure, or the physical realization.

pages.title: The cash-register example
pages.c: **A cash register illustrates how one function can have different physical implementations.** At the computational level, it determines the total price and the change due from a payment. At the algorithmic level, addition combines prices and subtraction determines change. Mechanical machinery, an electronic register, and a computer-based payment system can all carry out these functions.
support: The physical devices differ, but the arithmetic relation between the inputs and the required answer remains the same. This makes the problem suitable for explaining why an abstract task description can remain stable across implementations.
The algorithmic description specifies how the numbers are transformed. The implementational description specifies what actually performs those transformations.
pages.d: For the same prices and payment, the required amount of change is fixed by the task. Changing from a mechanical register to software changes the machinery, while preserving the input-output relation the cash-register function must satisfy.
pages.visual: The mechanical register, electronic register, and card-based payment images represent different realizations of the same transaction function. Their visible physical differences belong to implementation, while summing prices and computing change describe the operations.

pages.title: Treating language as a Type I problem
pages.c: **A Type I theory separates the abstract computation from the details of its realization.** Treating language this way allows a researcher to characterize grammatical knowledge and the procedures associated with it while setting aside such performance factors as memory constraints, errors, and associative learning. The proposed grammar is studied as a system in its own right.
support: This approach gives priority to determining what the linguistic system computes. Psychological processing and biological implementation then have to realize that characterization.

Chomsky’s critique preceded Marr’s account by about a decade. Marr’s framework provides a way to describe the theoretical separation, rather than being the historical source of Chomsky’s original argument.
pages.d: The Type I assumption is substantive. It proposes that an informative abstract characterization can be established independently enough from processing details to guide an account of those details.

pages.title: Type II theories and interacting processes
pages.c: **A Type II theory describes an ability through the interaction of the processes that produce it.** Marr allowed that some biological problems may resist a clean separation between an abstract computation and its realization. When many processes operate together, their interaction may be the simplest useful account of what the system does.
support: A Type I account begins with a characterization of the task that guides the choice of algorithms. A Type II account treats the organization and interaction of the processes as central to the explanation itself.
This is a contrast in explanatory structure. The issue is whether a separate abstract theory captures the ability adequately or whether the working system has to be described more directly.
pages.d: The phrase “whose interaction is its own simplest description” makes the key claim. The combined activity is not merely a complication added to an otherwise complete abstract theory. It is the phenomenon that the theory has to characterize.
pages.visual: The scanned quotation first identifies Chomsky’s competence theory with the computational level, then introduces Type II as an alternative for biological information processing. The contrast depends on the relation between the complete ability and its component processes.

pages.title: Language as a possible Type II system
pages.c: **Language transforms a complex internal organization of information into a sequence that another person can interpret.** The speaker produces an utterance one part after another, and the listener reconstructs an approximation of the intended information. Marr’s discussion raises the possibility that the constraints on this process arise from the mechanisms doing that work.
support: On this possibility, syntactic regularities could reflect effective ways to serialize and recover information. They would be connected to the functioning of the system, rather than forming a fully independent abstract theory.
The contrast is between treating grammatical structure as the starting specification and treating it as a useful description of regularities produced by interacting processes.
pages.d: A spoken sequence is one-dimensional in time, while the information being conveyed contains relations that are not simply a list. Explaining how this transformation works can therefore make memory, representation, and processing central to an account of grammar.
pages.visual: The quotation moves from the transformation into a sequential utterance to the listener’s reconstruction. It then explicitly proposes that natural-language grammar may have a Type II rather than a Type I theory.

pages.title: Why implementation may matter to language theory
pages.c: **The organization of the brain may shape the organization of language itself.** If linguistic behavior emerges from interacting processes, facts about learning, memory, perception, and action become part of an explanation of linguistic structure. The physical and psychological implementation then contributes to what the system can represent and do.
support: This possibility motivates an alternative to studying grammar as an independent symbolic system. The aim becomes to explain how the properties of the processing system generate the regularities observed in language use.
pages.d: The theoretical choice concerns where an explanation starts. One approach starts with an abstract grammar to be implemented. The alternative starts with properties of the learner and processing system and asks what language-like organization can develop.

pages.title: Distributed representations and gradual learning
pages.c: **Emergentist and parallel distributed processing approaches explain language through patterns of activity and gradual changes in connections.** A representation can be distributed over a group of units rather than located in a single symbol. Learning changes the strengths of connections, so experience alters how a pattern of input gives rise to a pattern of activity.
support: The neural analogy concerns activity across groups of neurons and changes in synaptic influence. It motivates examining the microstructure of a system, including how many small interactions together produce a larger regularity.
These approaches use a more graded relation among levels of analysis. Properties of the learning mechanism and representation are expected to shape the apparent rules in behavior.
pages.d: A distributed pattern can capture degrees of similarity between items. Gradual adjustment allows related experiences to influence later responses without requiring the system to add a new explicit rule for every case.

pages.title: Elman’s simple recurrent network
pages.c: **Elman’s 1990 simple recurrent network learns to predict the next item in a sequence.** The current input activates hidden units, which contribute to an output prediction. A copy of the hidden activation is carried into context units. That context supplies information about the preceding sequence when the next input arrives.
support: Learning adjusts the trainable connections so that the output prediction improves with experience. The task gives the network a reason to develop internal states that preserve useful information about order.
Because the same input can follow different preceding sequences, prediction depends on both the current item and the context accumulated from earlier items.
pages.d: Recurrence gives the network a limited history of its own processing. Its response to the current item can therefore differ according to what came before. The model is trained on prediction, and linguistic organization is investigated in the representations that develop.
pages.visual: The input and context units both feed the hidden units, and the hidden units feed the output. The curved solid connection copies hidden activity into context. Dotted connections are trainable, while the copying connection is fixed.

pages.title: Word boundaries from letter prediction
pages.c: **A letter-prediction network can develop sensitivity to word boundaries without being given spaces.** In the continuous sequence beginning “manyyearsagoaboyandgirl,” prediction becomes easier within a familiar word. Prediction error falls as the internal letters constrain what can follow, then often rises at the start of a new word.
support: The network’s task is to predict the next letter, rather than to label words directly. Repeated patterns within words provide information that improves prediction, while a boundary opens up more possibilities for what comes next.
The important result is that word-like organization appears in performance on the prediction task. An explicit instruction to divide the input into words is not the learning objective.
pages.d: The sequence contains both regularity and uncertainty. Recognizing a familiar beginning helps predict the rest of a word, while predicting the next word is harder. Changes in error across the sequence reveal that difference.
pages.visual: The horizontal progression follows successive letters, with each plotted point labeled by its letter. The vertical measure is prediction error. Peaks and declines align with the beginnings and interiors of words in the unspaced sentence, rather than showing a simple decline across training time.

pages.title: Grammatical and semantic grouping from prediction
pages.c: **Learning to predict words in simple sentences can produce internal representations that group words by grammatical and semantic properties.** Elman examined the hidden activation patterns associated with different words. Words that occurred in similar predictive contexts developed similar internal representations, even though the task was next-word prediction rather than explicit classification.
support: The resulting grouping distinguishes nouns from verbs and also separates meaningful subgroups. Nouns include animate and inanimate groups, with further clusters for humans, animals, food, and breakable things.
The verb group distinguishes patterns of direct-object use. These relationships matter because knowing what type of item has occurred helps predict what kinds of items can follow.
pages.d: The categories are an outcome of learning the sequence task. Similarity in hidden activity reflects the predictive role of an item across its contexts. Examining that similarity makes it possible to study what organization the network acquired.
pages.visual: The branching diagram clusters hidden-unit activation patterns. Short joining branches connect more similar patterns. Nouns and verbs occupy broad branches, and labels such as ANIMATES, FOOD, and BREAKABLES identify finer noun groupings. D.O. labels separate verbs by direct-object patterns.

pages.title: Statistical models and novel sentences
pages.c: **A statistical model can distinguish a grammatical novel sentence from a scrambled version by learning patterns across other sentences.** The whole string “Colorless green ideas sleep furiously” may be new, while its parts and the relations among word categories still reflect experience. A corpus supplies many examples from which those relations can be estimated.
support: Norvig’s discussion cites earlier occurrences of combinations such as “green ideas” and “ideas sleep.” It also describes Pereira’s 2001 model, which combined a finite-state statistical approach with word categories and learning from newspaper text.

That model assigned the grammatical ordering a probability 200,000 times greater than the reversed ordering. The comparison challenges the inference that unfamiliar complete sentences are beyond statistical learning.
pages.d: Novelty of the complete sentence is different from novelty of every relation within it. Learning can capture regularities that transfer to combinations never encountered as wholes. The model’s probability comparison tests that distinction directly.
pages.visual: The original ordering and its reversed counterpart contain the same words. Their large probability difference therefore concerns how those words and their categories are arranged. The historical phrase examples establish that several smaller combinations existed before the complete sentence was introduced.

pages.title: Speaker-series announcement
Two traditions in psycholinguistics
pages.c: **The symbolic and emergentist traditions differ in what they assume linguistic knowledge is.** A GOFAI, modular, or Chomskyan approach treats it as fundamentally abstract and symbolic, with linguistic representations differing in kind from other knowledge. An emergentist approach treats apparent symbols and rules as regularities that develop through learning and use.
support: In the symbolic tradition, psycholinguistics examines how an abstract system connects with perception, memory, and action. Those capacities allow linguistic knowledge to be used in real behavior.

In the emergentist tradition, those capacities help shape the representations themselves. Explaining language use therefore also means explaining how general psychological processes produce its organization.
pages.d: The disagreement is not simply whether people learn or whether language has regularities. It is whether the regularities are best explained through a distinct abstract system or through properties of the processes that learn and use language.

pages.title: Reading and speech-error assignment
Optional documentary recommendations
Variation across levels of language
pages.c: **Language contains graded patterns and variation at several levels.** Speech categories depend on multiple probabilistic cues. Words can support multiple interpretations. English past-tense formation includes regular patterns and forms such as RUN–RAN and SLEEP–SLEPT. Syntactic patterns also vary across speakers and dialects and change over time.
support: These facts motivate approaches that allow experience to shape graded expectations. A learning system has to accommodate both a strong recurring pattern and systematic departures from that pattern.

The challenge spans sounds, words, morphology, and sentence organization. It cannot be solved merely by assuming that every linguistic category has a single fixed boundary or that every pattern has an exceptionless verbal rule.
pages.d: A productive regularity and variation can coexist. The English past tense offers a particularly concrete case because adding -ed is useful for many verbs while familiar irregular forms remain part of speakers’ knowledge.
pages.visual: RUN–RAN and SLEEP–SLEPT illustrate different departures from the ordinary -ed pattern. They are morphological examples, while the other listed cases concern phonetic categories, lexical ambiguity, and syntactic variation.

pages.title: Moravec’s paradox
pages.c: **Moravec’s paradox reverses ordinary intuitions about which abilities are computationally difficult.** Formal tasks such as proving theorems or solving geometry problems can be comparatively manageable for a computer. Recognizing a face or moving across a room without collisions can be much harder, even though these perceptual and motor abilities feel easy to people.
support: The contrast questions whether formal rational problem solving provides a complete model of intelligence. Human cognition includes capacities that are sophisticated precisely because they usually operate without deliberate step-by-step reasoning.
For language research, this motivates taking perceptual, motor, and other processing systems seriously rather than treating them as simple attachments to a symbolic grammar.
pages.d: Ease for a human and ease for a programmed system can come apart. A person’s familiarity with an ability does not reveal the complexity of the processes that make it work.

pages.title: Family resemblance and fuzzy categories
pages.c: **Members of a category can overlap in different properties without sharing one defining feature.** Wittgenstein’s example is the category of games. Board games, card games, ball games, and Olympic games have many similarities, but examining their variety makes it difficult to identify one property that belongs to every member.
support: A family-resemblance account treats category membership as a network of overlapping similarities. One pair of games may share a feature that another pair lacks, while another property links that second pair to additional members.
This challenges a view in which every useful category must be defined by one strict list of necessary properties.
pages.d: The question is what keeps a category coherent when its members differ. Overlapping similarities can connect the members without requiring each one to match an identical checklist.
pages.visual: The quoted passage compares board games, card games, and ball games. Its repeated movement from one kind to another makes the pattern of shared and changing features central to the argument.

pages.title: Overlapping similarities rather than one shared essence
pages.c: **A family-resemblance category forms a network of similarities that cross and overlap.** A game may involve amusement, winning and losing, competition, skill, luck, or other properties, but those properties do not occur in every game in the same combination. Some similarities connect whole activities, while others concern particular details.
support: Wittgenstein contrasts examples such as chess, tennis, and a child throwing a ball against a wall. Features that seemed central in one comparison can disappear in another while the activities remain recognizable as games.
This gives a way to think about graded category structure. Similarity can support a category even when a fixed definition fails to capture all its members.
pages.d: Category structure can be distributed over relations among examples. A person can recognize a resemblance between two cases while also recognizing that another member resembles each of them in a different respect.
pages.visual: The quotation’s contrast between chess, tennis, and solitary ball play makes competition, amusement, skill, and luck vary independently. The closing description of similarities “overlapping and criss-crossing” identifies the proposed organizing relation.

pages.title: Psychological alternatives to formal rational accounts
pages.c: **Research on perception, categorization, and decision making helped challenge an exclusively formal and rational account of cognition.** Roger Shepard studied perception, Eleanor Rosch studied categorization, and Daniel Kahneman and Amos Tversky studied judgment and decision making. These research areas emphasized similarity, graded structure, and judgments that were not captured by a simple idealized rational procedure.
support: This broader psychological context supports asking whether language also reflects similarity-based generalization and properties of actual processing. A theory of cognition must explain how people perform, including the organization that develops through experience.
pages.d: The named researchers represent different domains rather than one shared experiment. Their relevance here is the convergence of several lines of psychology on explanations that take actual representations and processing seriously.

questions.stem: What makes the Turing test a behavioral test of machine intelligence?
choices: An examiner judges a conversational partner from its responses.
The examiner compares the machine’s circuitry with neurons.
The machine must outperform every human at arithmetic.
The machine must reproduce a stored poem exactly.
questions.why: The examiner infers the nature of the conversational partner from interaction, rather than directly inspecting its implementation.

questions.stem: What does the General Problem Solver require from a formal problem representation?
choices: States, a goal, and procedures for transforming states.
Only a reward signal, with no representation of a goal.
A photographic record of every possible physical setting.
A complete remembered answer to every possible problem.
questions.why: Symbolic problem solving applies procedures to represented states in order to reach a goal.

questions.stem: Why are judgments about unfamiliar sentences important to Chomsky’s account?
choices: They reveal knowledge extending beyond previously encountered complete utterances.
They prove that the speaker has memorized every possible sentence.
They eliminate the need for any structural account of language.
They measure the reward attached to the exact utterance in childhood.
questions.why: A speaker can recognize a new sentence as grammatical, motivating a productive internal system rather than a list of experienced utterances.

questions.stem: What is held constant when “Colorless green ideas sleep furiously” is compared with its reversed ordering?
choices: The individual words.
The grammatical structure.
The order of adjectives and nouns.
The relation between the subject and the verb.
questions.why: The same lexical items are rearranged, so the judgment difference highlights organization rather than different vocabulary.

questions.stem: In the cash-register example, adding item prices belongs most directly to which level?
choices: Algorithmic.
Implementational.
The material composition of the device.
The social context of the purchase.
questions.why: Addition is an operation used to solve the transaction problem. The computational level specifies the task, while implementation concerns the machinery.

questions.stem: What is distinctive about a Type II explanation?
choices: The interaction of component processes is central to the simplest useful account.
An abstract function is always fully independent of its processing mechanisms.
A system must contain exactly two mental processes.
All observable errors are excluded before the theory is constructed.
questions.why: Marr’s Type II possibility concerns cases where the interacting processes themselves provide the relevant explanation.

questions.stem: What do the context units contribute to Elman’s simple recurrent network?
choices: A copy of previous hidden activity that influences the next prediction.
A list of explicit word boundaries supplied by the experimenter.
A fixed grammatical-category label for every input word.
A second output unrelated to the preceding sequence.
questions.why: Context units carry hidden activity forward so that prediction can depend on sequence history.

questions.stem: What does falling prediction error within words indicate in the unspaced letter sequence?
choices: Internal letter sequences become more predictable as the word unfolds.
The graph records only a general decrease across training sessions.
The network was given a space before every word.
The network directly received a noun or verb label at each letter.
questions.why: The horizontal progression follows letters, and error often falls within a word. The learning task was next-letter prediction rather than explicit segmentation.

questions.stem: How did grammatical and semantic groupings arise in the sentence-prediction network?
choices: Similar predictive contexts led to similar hidden representations.
The model was trained solely to copy category labels.
An investigator assigned each hidden unit a complete word in advance.
A rule required every noun to occupy an identical local symbol.
questions.why: The task was sequence prediction. Groupings were found by analyzing the hidden activation patterns that developed during learning.

choices: Formal proofs can be easier for computers than ordinary perception and movement.
Every task humans find easy is equally easy to program.
Face recognition is easier to formalize than every logical puzzle.
Human conversation depends only on explicit logical deduction.
questions.why: The paradox concerns the difference between apparent ease for people and difficulty for computational systems, especially in perception and action.

written.prompt: Use the cash-register example to distinguish Marr’s three levels, then explain what changes in a Type II approach.
answer: The computational description specifies the transaction problem and required result. The algorithmic description specifies operations such as addition and subtraction. The implementation describes the machinery performing them.
A Type II approach treats the interaction of underlying processes as central to the explanation, rather than assuming that a fully independent abstract description captures the ability.

written.prompt: Explain how Elman’s prediction task produced evidence relevant to word boundaries and grammatical categories.
answer: A recurrent network uses current input and prior hidden activity to predict the next item. In unspaced letter sequences, prediction error often falls within words and rises at boundaries.

With sentence input, hidden activation patterns cluster according to grammatical and semantic relationships. These organizations develop through prediction learning rather than direct training on word boundaries or category labels.
